1:
Clarke opens with the arithmetic: Jehoahaz began at the commencement of the twenty-third year of Joash and reigned seventeen years, fourteen alone and three alongside his own son, the fourteenth being but just begun. Gill adds only that this was the year Joash was busy repairing the temple. On the prayer Ellicott takes the verb literally, that Jehoahaz stroked the face of the Lord, a metaphor that occurs also at Exodus 32:11; and he insists that the hearkening was not immediate, since the Syrian invasions were renewed again and again throughout the reign and the tide only turned under Joash, whose incomplete victories were followed by the permanent successes of the next generation. Gill guards it differently, denying that it was heard for the king's sake or for his repentance and humiliation, which were only external, but because Israel were oppressed and were still God's people;.

Who the promised saviour was divides them flatly. Gill rules out four candidates in a line, not an angel, nor a captain raised up among them, nor Elisha who merely predicted the deliverance, nor Jehoahaz himself, but his son Joash; Clarke says Joash undoubtedly, pointing to the wars at the end of the chapter. Ellicott looks a generation further and makes it the grandson, of whom it is said in the following chapter that the Lord saved Israel by his hand. The same stretch has a structural problem two witnesses solve alike and a third by rearrangement. Gill and Ellicott both read the intervening verses as a parenthesis and the fifty horsemen as resuming the sentence about the prayer, while Clarke reports Houbigant's recommendation that they be read in another order, the seventh after the fourth and then the fifth and sixth. On the subject of that resumed clause the two part company: Gill makes it the king of Syria, who left Israel's king no more than fifty horsemen out of his army, while Ellicott takes it to be the Lord himself.

At the grove the comments converge on identification and diverge on blame. Ellicott renders it that the Asherah stood, or was set up, in Samaria, and explains it as the sacred tree often depicted in Assyrian art, symbolising the productive principle of nature and sacred to Ashtoreth; with peace and prosperity, he adds, luxury soon reappeared and the idolatry that countenanced it lifted up its head again. Clarke names the same figure under both her names and says only that she remained in Samaria, worshipped with all her abominable rites. Wesley fixes the blame earlier, on Ahab who planted the grove for the worship of Baal and on the failure to destroy it as the law required. Ellicott then ventures what none of the others does: this verdict on the northern worship is written from the standpoint of an editor living long after the events, and it does not appear from the histories of Elijah and Elisha incorporated in his work that either prophet ever protested against the worship established at Bethel and Dan.

Ellicott reads the small remnant of cavalry as evidence, not rhetoric. So few appears to indicate losses in some great battle or in successive engagements, and since the Syrians were especially strong in chariots and horsemen the destruction of just those forces amounted to complete disarmament; the clause about threshing he would render instead that Israel was set like the dust to be trampled underfoot. On the closing notices the readings are textual. Ellicott glosses the might as prowess, and renders the sleeping with his fathers as lying down like them, noting the same phrase is used even of a king who came to a violent end. Wesley draws the inference that matters: though Jehoahaz had no success he showed much personal valour, noted to intimate that Israel was not conquered through any cowardice in its king but merely by the righteous judgment of God.
10:
The regnal date will not reconcile itself, and the three attempts on it differ in kind. Gill harmonises, supposing either that two of the years were imperfect or, as he prefers, that the son reigned two or three years in his father's lifetime, so that Jehoahaz lived to see his prayer answered. Clarke harmonises the same way on Calmet's authority, making Joash associated with his father two years before his death, the sixteen years including the joint reign. Ellicott declines to harmonise at all: the figure does not agree with the earlier notice, and the reading of one Greek manuscript tradition, thirty-ninth, is simply right.

At the sickness the comments gather round two facts, his age and his death. Gill states the plain one, that the prophets do not live for ever and that Elisha died rather than being translated as Elijah was. Clarke dates the illness to the tenth year of Joash and reckons that Elisha must have prophesied some sixty-five years, where Wesley makes it sixty from his first call. Both Clarke and Ellicott notice that the king's cry is the very cry Elisha himself had raised at Elijah's translation, and Ellicott reads it as Joash lamenting the loss of his best counsellor, the prophet having been more to Israel than chariots and horsemen.

On the archery Ellicott is the only one who attends to how a bow is actually held: the left hand rides upon it while the right grasps arrow and string, so that the king's hand is the left. The prophet's hands laid over the king's he reads as investing the act of shooting with a prophetic character; and adds that it is not implied the prophet's hands were still on the king's when the arrow flew. On the eastward window Gill raises an objection the others do not: the Jewish commentators generally put Syria east of Israel, but it lay northeast or rather more north, so that the direction may instead concern the eastward part of Israel which the Syrians had taken. Clarke takes the simpler view that the window faced the country beyond Jordan which Hazael had seized, and supplies the custom behind it: it was ancient practice to shoot an arrow or cast a spear into a country an army intended to invade, as Alexander threw a dart on reaching the enemy's coast, and as the Roman herald declared war at the enemy's frontier and threw in a spear. Ellicott renders the saying itself as an arrow of victory for the Lord and an arrow of victory over Aram, and notes that what is predicted is the annihilation of the opposing army at Aphek and not of the entire forces of Syria.

The three strokes and the anger are handled most fully by Ellicott, who sets the scene in its ancient context. Soothsaying by means of arrows, he says, was a practice of unknown antiquity in that world; the arrows of David and Jonathan were an instance of the same thing, which in principle is analogous to casting lots. On that reading the prophet left the number of strokes to the king's spontaneous impulse because he believed the result would betoken the purpose of God, and his anger was that of the man and the patriot, disappointed at a divination from which he had hoped greater things; the irritability of a sick man, Ellicott allows, may have contributed too. Gill reaches the same place by another route, that the prophet knew the number of strokes would measure the number of victories but that the choice was left to the king, so that the prophet would learn from it with what spirit the king would pursue his advantages. Clarke adds the guard the episode needs: Elisha's being wroth at three instead of five or six does not prove that God was wroth, or that he had ever intended more.
20:
Where Elisha was buried and how long he prophesied are both disputed, and Gill lays the authorities out. Epiphanius puts the grave in a city of Samaria, the Jews on Mount Carmel in the cave of Elijah. The Jewish chronology places his death in the tenth year of Joash after more than sixty years of prophesying, which Abarbinel makes sixty-six; but Gill ends by preferring Kimchi, that he died at the beginning of Joash's reign and even before his father's death, while the son was still partner in the throne.

Clarke uses the death notice to compare the two prophets, and ventures what none of the others would: of Elijah he says it is hard to tell whether he was a man or an angel in a human body, the arguments for the latter being strong and the objections feeble, and he answers the obvious objection that being fed by an angel proves nothing, since God manifest in the flesh was fed by the same ministry. Elisha he holds not less eminent, his miracles various and stupendous; and he quotes the old character of him, that after his death his body prophesied, which he takes of the raising that follows. Ellicott works on the raiders in the same verse, rendering it that troops of Moabites used to invade, revenging the devastation of their own country; and on the time of year he supposes a preposition has fallen out, so that it reads when the year came in, that is in the spring.

The revived man draws a reconstruction from Clarke and a textual note from Ellicott. Clarke has the burial party catch sight of a marauding band and, through fear, throw the body into Elisha's grave, which chanced then to be open. He concludes first that the prophet worked no miracle by his own power but by God's, who honoured his servant by making even his bones the instrument of another miracle after death. He concludes second that this is the first and, he believes, the last true miracle performed by the bones of a dead man, and yet on it the whole system of miraculous working relics has been built. Ellicott attends to the order of the words, backing Houbigant's conjecture that the text says they departed and then that the man touched the bones, rather than that the man went and touched them. He adds that the tomb must have been the more easily opened because the action was done in haste, and reports Thenius's view that the miracle was a pledge of Elisha's promise to the king.

At the closing notices Ellicott reads the historian rather than the history: the verse about God being gracious he takes for a remark of the compiler's, evident from its style, from the appeal to the covenant and from the phrase as yet, which means rather until now, the day he was writing, when the northern kingdom had already perished. Clarke takes the same verse devotionally, working its three verbs: God had tender affection for them as a husband for his wife, his bowels yearned over them, and he turned his face towards them again, the covenant forbidding that the people be utterly destroyed when the Messiah was to come from them. On the successor Gill explains that this was the third of the name, the first of the Damascene kings, the name being kept as respectable with the Syrians although the kingdom had passed to another family; Ellicott adds that this king is absent from the Assyrian records, that the name was a divine title implying no connection with the dynasty Hazael overthrew, and that he was probably feebler than his father. The recovered cities divide them to the last: Gill places them in Gilead and Bashan, while Ellicott argues they must have lain west of Jordan, the trans-Jordan having been subdued in the time of Jehu.
